questions.stem: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heart rate is 180 beats per minute, and his ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. He is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following interventions can be used to terminate this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents to the emergency department with palpitations and shortness of breath. His heart rate is 180 beats per minute, and his ECG shows narrow-complex tachycardia with no visible P waves. He is diagnosed with paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. Which of the following interventions can be used to terminate this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Valsalva manoeuvre: Vagal manoeuvres are simple techniques used to terminate an episode of PSVT by stimulating the vagus nerve, which slows down the heart rate. These manoeuvres are safe and effective for most patients and can be performed in inpatient and outpatient settings. Some examples of vagal manoeuvres include: Valsalva manoeuvre: This involves forcefully exhaling against a closed airway ( e.g., by pinching the nose and closing the mouth) for 10-15 seconds. This increases intrathoracic pressure , stimulating the vagus nerve and slowing the heart rate. Carotid sinus massage: This involves applying gentle pressure to the carotid artery in the neck for 5-10 seconds. This can activate the baroreceptor reflex, which slows down the heart rate. Cold water immersion of the face involves splashing cold water on the face or immersing the face in cold water for a few seconds. This stimulates the trigeminal nerve, stimulating the vagus nerve and slows the heart rate. Gagging: This involves stimulating the gag reflex by touching the back of the throat with a tongue depressor or toothbrush. This can activate the vagus nerve and slow down the heart rate. Vagal manoeuvres are generally safe, but they should not be performed in patients with certain conditions, such as carotid artery disease, a history of stroke, or glaucoma. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pneumatic compression stockings: Pneumatic compression stockings, also known as compression stockings or compression socks, are commonly used to prevent deep vein thrombosis in hospitalized patients. They work by applying pressure to the legs to improve blood flow. While they can be beneficial for preventing blood clots, they are ineffective in terminating an episode of PSVT. Option C - Oxygen therapy: Oxygen therapy is commonly used in the emergency department to treat hypoxia or respiratory distress. While it can be helpful in certain situations, it is ineffective for terminating an episode of PSVT. Option D - Intravenous fluids: Intravenous fluids may be used in the emergency department to correct hypovolemia or electrolyte imbalances, which can contribute to developing PSVT. However, they are not effective in terminating an episode of PSVT. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old female with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with metabolic acidosis. She is being treated with the following medications. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for the development of metabolic acidosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old female with a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) presents with metabolic acidosis. She is being treated with the following medications. Which of the following drugs is most likely responsible for the development of metabolic acidosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Metformin Metformin is a biguanide oral hypoglycemic agent used in the management of type 2 diabetes mellitus. The most common side effect of metformin is gastrointestinal disturbance. However, it can also cause lactic acidosis in rare cases, especially in patients with impaired renal function. Metformin-induced lactic acidosis is a type of metabolic acidosis that occurs due to the accumulation of lactic acid in the body. Incorrect options: Option B: Salbutamol Salbutamol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist used in the treatment of asthma and COPD. Trembling, headache, palpitations and muscle cramps are adverse effects of salbutamol. It does not typically cause metabolic acidosis as a side effect. Option C: Ibuprofen Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug ( NSAID ) used for pain relief and inflammation. Interstitial nephritis, gastric ulcer (prostaglandins protect gastric mucosa), renal ischemia (prostaglandins vasodilate afferent arteriole), aplastic anaemia are adverse effects of ibuprofen. It does not typically cause metabolic acidosis as a side effect. Option D: Alendronate Alendronate is a bisphosphonate used for the treatment of osteoporosis and other bone diseases. questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman comes to the physician due to a one-month history of weight gain and facial oedema. Her blood pressure is 140/80 mm Hg, her pulse is 80/min, and her examination shows 2+ ankle oedema. Urine analysis shows 3+ proteinuria and fatty casts. Which of the following is most likely the cause of her proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Glomerular proteinuria The patient, in this case, has nephrotic syndrome. Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome characterized by the following: Proteinuria (> 3-3.5 g/day - most important manifestation) Hypoalbuminemia Edema Hyperlipidemia and lipiduria The basic pathology is the altered permeability of the glomerular membrane for proteins. Diseases most commonly causing nephrotic syndrome are: Minimal change disease (in children) Membranous glomerulopathy (adults) Mesangial proliferative glomerulonephritis Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis Proteinuria is excessive protein excretion in the urine, generally greater than 150 mg daily in adults. Proteinuria can be associated with high serum creatinine levels, elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN) or evidence of systemic illness (e.g., fever, rash, vasculitis). Glomerular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the glomerular filtration barrier in the kidneys. The glomerular filtration barrier is a complex structure comprising three layers: the fenestrated endothelium, the basement membrane, and the podocytes. This barrier is responsible for filtering out waste products and excess fluid from the blood while preventing larger molecules, such as proteins, from entering the urine. Glomerular proteinuria can occur when there is damage or disruption to any of these layers, which can lead to the passage of protein into the urine. It results from the effacement of epithelial cell foot processes and altered glomerular permeability with an increased filtration fraction of normal plasma proteins, as in diabetic nephropathy. Protein electrophoresis will have a pattern exhibiting a large albumin spike indicative of the increased permeability of albumin across the damaged GBM. Incorrect options: Option A: Functional proteinuria Functional proteinuria is not due to any underlying disease or medical condition but a functional body response to certain stressors. This type of proteinuria is usually benign and self-limiting and does not require any specific treatment. Functional proteinuria can be caused by a variety of factors, including: Exercise Fever Emotional stress Dehydration Functional proteinuria is a benign process resulting from acute illness, exercise, and "orthostatic proteinuria." Orthostatic proteinuria usually causes protein excretion of less than 1 g/day. It occurs only during the daytime and is associated with an upright posture. This patient has a history of nephrotic syndrome, so functional proteinuria is unlikely. Option C: Tubular proteinuria Tubular proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormalities in the reabsorption of proteins by the tubular cells in the kidneys. Normally, the kidney tubular cells reabsorb small amounts of protein that pass through the glomeruli and into the filtrate. However, in tubular proteinuria, there is a defect in the tubular cells that impairs their ability to reabsorb proteins, leading to increased protein levels in the urine. It occurs as the reabsorption of normally filtered proteins in the proximal tubule is defective. It occurs due to a variety of causes: Acute tubular necrosis Toxic injury (lead, aminoglycosides and certain antiretrovirals), Drug-induced interstitial nephritis Hereditary metabolic disorders (Wilson disease and Fanconi syndrome). Option D: Overload proteinuria Overload proteinuria is a medical condition characterized by excess protein in the urine due to abnormal blood proteins that exceed the renal tubules' reabsorptive capacity. In this type of proteinuria, the excess protein is not due to a defect in the glomerular filtration barrier or tubular reabsorption but rather due to an excess of abnormal proteins that the renal tubules cannot properly reabsorb. Overload proteinuria can result from: Overproduction of circulating, filterable plasma proteins (monoclonal gammopathies), such as Bence Jones proteins associated with plasma cell myeloma (formerly multiple myeloma). Amyloidosis: Amyloidosis is a condition in which abnormal proteins build up in various tissues in the body, including the kidneys, and can lead to overflow proteinuria. Sickle cell disease: Sickle cell disease can cause the breakdown of red blood cells, releasing hemoglobin into the blood and urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Fabry disease: It is a genetic disorder in which a buildup of a specific type of fat in the body can produce abnormal proteins that can be excreted in the urine, leading to overflow proteinuria. Protein electrophoresis from the serum or urine will exhibit a discrete protein peak. Other examples of overload proteinuria include myoglobinuria in rhabdomyolysis and hemoglobinuria in hemolysis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower extremity oedema. Physical exam reveals jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 gallop. His serum BNP level is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old male with a history of hypertension presents to the emergency department with dyspnea, orthopnea, and bilateral lower extremity oedema. Physical exam reveals jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 gallop. His serum BNP level is elevated. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Heart failure: The clinical presentation of dyspnea, orthopnea, bilateral lower extremity oedema, jugular venous distension, bibasilar crackles, and an S3 gallop, in addition to an elevated serum BNP level, are highly suggestive of heart failure. Heart failure is a common clinical syndrome that occurs as a result of the heart's inability to pump enough blood to meet the body's metabolic demands. It can be caused by several factors, including hypertension, coronary artery disease, valvular disease, and cardiomyopathy. Incorrect Options: Option A- Acute myocardial infarction: Acute myocardial infarction (AMI) can cause heart failure, but it typically presents with chest pain, electrocardiographic changes, and elevated cardiac biomarkers, such as troponin. In this case, the patient did not present with chest pain, and his troponin level was not mentioned, making AMI an unlikely diagnosis. Option B- Aortic stenosis: Aortic stenosis is a condition where the aortic valve narrows, leading to reduced blood flow from the left ventricle to the aorta. Patients with aortic stenosis may present with chest pain, syncope, and dyspnea on exertion. However, in this case, the patient’s presented with orthopnea and bilateral lower extremity oedema, which are not typical symptoms of aortic stenosis, making it an unlikely diagnosis. Option C- Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a life-threatening condition that occurs when a blood clot travels to the lungs, obstructing blood flow. Patients with PE typically present with sudden onset dyspnea, chest pain, tachycardia, and hypoxemia. While heart failure can occur as a complication of PE, it would not be the most likely diagnosis given the patient's presentation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following patients has the highest likelihood of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion resulting in transfusion refractoriness?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following patients has the highest likelihood of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion resulting in transfusion refractoriness?

options.label: A
options.text: 52 year old G0P0 female with her husband as the platelet donor

options.label: B
options.text: 52 year old G0P0 female with a random platelet donor

options.label: C
options.text: 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor

options.label: D
options.text: 52 year old G4P4 female with a random platelet donor

questions.answerText: 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor
questions.solution: Correct Option C - 52 year old G4P4 female with her son as the platelet donor: Generally, multiparous women are more likely than men or nulliparous women to develop alloimmunization to platelets. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor puts her at an even higher risk, as she may have developed antibodies to the child's father's HLA antigens during her pregnancy. Most cases (~2/3) of platelet refactoriness are NOT due to alloimmunization. However, in cases that are, most are due to antibodies that are created in response to HLA class I antigens on leukocytes or platelets. These antibodies can exist in multiparous women due to maternal-fetal HLA incompatibility during pregnancy. Fetal HLA class I antigens inherited from the father are recognized by the mother as foreign. Multiple pregnancies will put the patient at a higher risk of developing such antibodies. Furthermore, receiving a transfusion with her son as the donor greatly increases the risk of re-presenting HLA class I antigens to antibodies which she has developed.Platelet alloimmunization can also occur in patients who have received multiple transfusions or due to antibodies to platelet specific antigens (human platelet antigens). Incorrect Options: Option A - 52-year-old G0P0 female with her husband as the platelet donor: Alloimmunization to platelet transfusion is more common in multiparous women, as they are exposed to foreign HLA antigens during pregnancy. In this case, the patient has not been pregnant before (G0P0), which lowers her likelihood of developing alloantibodies. Additionally, her husband's HLA antigens are less likely to trigger an immune response compared to antigens from her own offspring. Option B - 52 -year-old G0P0 female with a random platelet donor: This patient is also a nulliparous woman (G0P0), reducing her risk of developing alloimmunization to platelet transfusion. The likelihood of developing alloantibodies is higher in multiparous women due to exposure to foreign HLA antigens during pregnancy. Option D - 52-year-old G4P4 female with a random platelet donor: While this patient is multiparous (G4P4) and has a higher likelihood of developing alloantibodies, the key difference compared to option C is the donor. In this case, the donor is random, meaning the donor's HLA antigens are not specifically associated with those of her offspring. The risk of developing antibodies against random donor HLA antigens is lower compared to antibodies against her son's HLA antigens. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 60-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his son after he found him lying on the ground. The patient is unable to speak and is unable to walk properly. Physical examination reveals an irregular pulse, weakness of the left upper and lower extremities, and aphasia. His medical history is significant for diabetes, COPD and hypertension all of which are well-controlled by medications. An ECG is performed and shown below. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male is brought to the emergency department by his son after he found him lying on the ground. The patient is unable to speak and is unable to walk properly. Physical examination reveals an irregular pulse, weakness of the left upper and lower extremities, and aphasia. His medical history is significant for diabetes, COPD and hypertension all of which are well-controlled by medications. An ECG is performed and shown below. Which of the following interventions could have prevented this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B- Prophylactic anticoagulation: This patient with acute onset left-sided weakness and aphasia is most likely suffering from a stroke, particularly an embolic stroke in light of this patient’s underlying atrial fibrillation as proven by the ECG findings. Pathogenesis of A-fib is characterized by abnormal automatic firing and the presence of multiple interacting reentry circuits looping around the atria. Episodes of AF are initiated by rapid bursts of ectopic beats arising from conducting tissue in the pulmonary veins or from diseased/dilated atrial tissue. Atrial fibrillation most commonly occurs due to atrial remodeling as a result of hypertension (as in this patient) and other cardiac disorders e.g. mitral stenosis. Atrial fibrillation results in stasis of blood flow in the left atrium . As a result, there is an increased risk of thrombus formation in the left atrial appendage. This thrombus can subsequently embolize into the systemic circulation and lead to ischemia of the affected region. The risk of thrombosis can be reduced by the use of anticoagulation that prevents the formation of clots that eventually lodge in the distal circulation. Incorrect Options: Option A- Synchronized cardioversion: This treatment modality is used to terminate atrial fibrillation that leads to hemodynamic instability i.e. hypotension. It cannot mitigate the risk of thrombosis. Option C- Defibrillation: This intervention is used to terminate ventricular fibrillation It has no role in A-fib Option D- Angioplasty: Angioplasty is done in cases of myocardial infarction which presents as chest pain radiating to the neck and left arm, diaphoresis, and an impending sense of doom. An MI presents with ST-elevations on ECG @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old patient with a history of recurrent cold sores caused by Herpes Simplex Virus type 1 (HSV-1) seeks further clarification about the virus's behavior. Which of the following statements best describes the characteristic of HSV-1 regarding latency?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old patient with a history of recurrent cold sores caused by Herpes Simplex Virus type 1 (HSV-1) seeks further clarification about the virus's behavior. Which of the following statements best describes the characteristic of HSV-1 regarding latency?

options.label: A
options.text: HSV-1 remains dormant in the spinal cord neurons.

options.label: B
options.text: The virus persists latently in the liver cells.

options.label: C
options.text: Latency is established in the trigeminal ganglia.

options.label: D
options.text: HSV-1 undergoes latency in the renal epithelial cells.

questions.answerText: Latency is established in the trigeminal ganglia.
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Latency is established in the trigeminal ganglia: After primary infection, HSV-1 establishes latency in sensory neurons, particularly the trigeminal ganglia. questions.stem: Which of the following is a regulatory protein that promotes cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is a regulatory protein that promotes cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Bcl-2 Bcl-2, also known as B-cell lymphoma 2, is an anti-apoptotic regulatory protein that plays a crucial role in promoting cell survival by inhibiting apoptosis. It is a member of the Bcl-2 family of proteins, which regulate the intrinsic or mitochondrial pathway of apoptosis. Bcl-2 is located in the outer mitochondrial membrane and functions to prevent the release of cytochrome c and other pro-apoptotic factors from the mitochondria, thus blocking the activation of the apoptosis cascade. By inhibiting the pro-apoptotic proteins such as BAX and BAK, Bcl-2 helps to maintain the integrity of the mitochondrial membrane and prevent cell death, promoting cell survival. Incorrect Options: Option A - BAX: BAX is a pro-apoptotic protein belonging to the Bcl-2 family. It promotes apoptosis by forming channels in the mitochondrial membrane, leading to the release of cytochrome c and initiating the apoptosis cascade. BAX acts opposite to Bcl-2 and promotes cell death. Option B - BAK: Like BAX, BAK is also a pro-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 family. It is involved in the permeabilization of the mitochondrial membrane and the release of cytochrome c, triggering apoptosis. BAK works similarly to BAX and promotes cell death. Option D - BAD: BAD is another pro-apoptotic protein belonging to the Bcl-2 family. It acts by binding and inhibiting anti-apoptotic proteins like Bcl-2 and Bcl-XL. Inhibition of these anti-apoptotic proteins can lead to the activation of pro-apoptotic proteins like BAX and BAK, promoting apoptosis. So, BAD is involved in promoting cell death rather than inhibiting it. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain  with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Transient synovitis: Transient synovitis and septic arthritis are the most common causes of atraumatic hip pain in children . Transient synovitis usually occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 8 years of age, most often in boys. Children typically have had symptoms for one to three days at presentation and will demonstrate an antalgic gait with an abducted and externally rotated hip at rest. Pain is exacerbated with internal rotation of the hip, although pain with motion is less severe than in children with septic arthritis of the hip. Referred pain to the knee may be the only complaint , so careful inspection of the hip is mandatory in all patients with isolated knee pain. Referred pain from the hip to knee is usually a dull pain that is located anteriorly and does not localize to bone or soft tissue. Examination of the knee is usually normal. The hip exam typically demonstrates a limited range of motion with pain. Serious causes of hip pain must be excluded, including septic arthritis, fracture, slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease. Patients with transient synovitis rarely have a fever Management of transient synovitis is purely supportive and includes rest and NSAIDs. Incorrect Options: Option A- Femoral neck fracture: Hip fracture in a paediatric patient is suggested by high-force trauma, and severe tenderness is common. Option B- Osteogenesis imperfecta: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a rare disease that causes problems in bone synthesis due to collagen defects. Frequent fractures are common, and a physical examination may demonstrate blue sclerae, deafness, and ligamentous laxity. Subclinical cases may be more common than previously recognized. Option D- Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE): SCFE occurs when the femoral epiphysis slips off the metaphysis, usually in adolescents. @Neet_pg_bot

The child appears healthy at birth but starts experiencing various infections shortly after. The child has chronic diarrhea and is failing to thrive. Physical examination reveals absent lymph nodes and tonsils. Laboratory tests show absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells. Thymic shadow is also absent on imaging. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of these clinical findings?
questions.stemHtml: A newborn infant is brought to the clinic by his parents due to recurrent and severe infections. The child appears healthy at birth but starts experiencing various infections shortly after. The child has chronic diarrhea and is failing to thrive. Physical examination reveals absent lymph nodes and tonsils. Laboratory tests show absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells. Thymic shadow is also absent on imaging. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of these clinical findings?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID): Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a group of rare, genetic disorders that result in a severe impairment of both cellular and humoral immunity. This means that both T cells and B cells are affected, leading to an inability to fight off infections. The absence of T cells, B cells, NK cells, and a thymic shadow on imaging strongly indicates SCID. There are several genetic causes of SCID, including mutations in genes involved in lymphocyte development and function. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyper IgM Syndrome: Hyper IgM Syndrome is a primary immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the inability of B cells to switch from producing IgM antibodies to other antibody classes (IgG, IgA, IgE), leading to elevated IgM levels and decreased levels of other antibody classes. It is typically caused by mutations in the CD40 ligand gene. While infections are common in Hyper IgM Syndrome, the absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells, along with the absent thymic shadow, points towards a more severe immunodeficiency condition than Hyper IgM Syndrome. Option B - Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked primary immunodeficiency disorder caused by mutations in the WAS gene, leading to defects in platelet function and immune cell signaling. It is characterized by thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), eczema, and recurrent infections. While it can lead to immune dysfunction, the absence of T cells, B cells, and NK cells, along with the absent thymic shadow, suggests a more profound immunodeficiency than Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome. Option D - Ataxia-Telangiectasia: Ataxia-Telangiectasia is a rare autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATM gene. It primarily affects the nervous system, leading to symptoms like progressive ataxia (lack of muscle control), telangiectasia (dilated blood vessels), and an increased risk of certain cancers. While Ataxia-Telangiectasia can also result in immune system dysfunction, the absence of lymph nodes, tonsils, and thymic shadow on imaging suggests a more profound immunodeficiency than what is typically seen in Ataxia-Telangiectasia. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following complications is associated with hyponatremia in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old female with a history of heart failure presents to the emergency department with altered mental status. Which of the following complications is associated with hyponatremia in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Cerebral edema: The patient in this clinical scenario has hyponatremia , defined as a serum sodium level below 135 mEq/L. Hyponatremia can cause cerebral edema due to an influx of water into the brain cells, leading to increased intracranial pressure and altered mental status. In this patient with a history of heart failure, the hyponatremia is likely due to the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion , which can occur in response to heart failure or other conditions. Treatment for hyponatremia in this patient includes water restriction and administration of hypertonic saline as appropriate. Incorrect Options: Option A- Hypertensive encephalopathy: Hypertensive encephalopathy is not associated with hyponatremia. Hypertensive encephalopathy is a rare but serious complication of high blood pressure that can cause headaches, confusion, seizures, and coma. It involves damage to the myelin sheath in the pons region of the brain and can lead to quadriplegia, pseudobulbar palsy, and locked-in syndrome. Option D - Renal failure: Renal failure can cause electrolyte imbalances, including hyponatremia, but it is not a complication associated with hyponatremia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Thymoma: Thymoma is the most likely diagnosis in this case. Thymomas are tumors that arise from the thymus gland in the anterior mediastinum. They can often be detected on a chest X-ray as a mass. The "thymic sail sign" refers to the appearance of the thymoma abutting the superior vena cava (SVC) and resembling the sail of a boat. Thymomas are typically slow-growing and may be asymptomatic or present with symptoms related to compression of nearby structures. Option C - Pulmonary embolism: Pulmonary embolism is a condition where a blood clot travels to the lungs, causing sudden symptoms like shortness of breath, chest pain, and rapid heart rate. It wouldn't typically present as a firm mediastinal mass with the thymic sail sign. Option D - Aortic aneurysm: An aortic aneurysm involves the dilation of the aorta, the main blood vessel leaving the heart. While it could present as a mediastinal mass, it wouldn't exhibit the thymic sail sign. Additionally, aortic aneurysms are more commonly found in older individuals and those with risk factors like hypertension. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: It is the most common of the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias

Streptococcus pneumoniae is the most common cause of CAP. The likelihood that other organisms may be involved depends on the age of the patient and the clinical scenario (previous illness, immunocompromised state, travel history, exposure to animals or contaminated water). Patients usually present with fever, rigours, chills, cough productive of mucopurulent sputum, pleuritis chest pain, and upper abdominal pain. His medical history is insignificant, except for excessive bleeding from the umbilical stump after birth, frequent nosebleeds, and easy bruising. Fibrin, fibrinogen, PT and aPTT are normal. However, a clot solubility assay using 2% acetic acid results in clot dissolution. What is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Factor XIII deficiency: Factor XIII is a coagulation factor responsible for stabilizing blood clots by cross-linking fibrin. A deficiency in Factor XIII can lead to impaired clot stability. The excessive bleeding from the umbilical stump after birth, frequent nosebleeds, easy bruising, and a recent intracranial bleed and hematoma following a fall, is characteristic of a bleeding disorder. The clot solubility assay using 2% acetic acid results in clot dissolution, which is a specific test for Factor XIII deficiency. In Factor XIII deficiency, clots are formed but lack the stability provided by cross-linking, making them susceptible to dissolution in acetic acid. Incorrect Options: Option A- Deficiency of fibrinogen: Fibrinogen is involved in the early stages of blood clot formation, and its deficiency typically results in prolonged PT and aPTT. questions.solution: Correct Option C- ACE inhibitors can be used in combination with potassium-sparing diuretics for the treatment of Bartter syndrome: Bartter syndrome is a rare inherited disorder that affects the kidneys and causes a deficiency of potassium and chloride ions in the body. The treatment of Bartter syndrome aims to correct the electrolyte imbalances and improve symptoms. Potassium supplementation is the initial management of hypokalemia in Bartter's syndrome, but it may not be enough to maintain normal potassium levels. ACE inhibitors are known to decrease aldosterone secretion and promote potassium retention, making them useful in the management of hyperkalemia in Bartter syndrome. ACE inhibitors can be used in combination with potassium-sparing diuretics to treat Bartter syndrome. This combination can help to maintain potassium levels and improve metabolic alkalosis. Incorrect Options: Option A- ACE inhibitors are not effective in treating Bartter syndrome: ACE inhibitors have been shown to be effective in the treatment of Bartter syndrome by blocking the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and reducing aldosterone secretion, which can lead to potassium wasting and metabolic alkalosis. Option B- ACE inhibitors should be used as the first-line treatment for Bartter syndrome: While ACE inhibitors are effective in treating Bartter syndrome, they are not considered first-line treatment. The initial treatment for Bartter syndrome typically involves increasing potassium intake and using potassium-sparing diuretics. Option D - ACE inhibitors should be avoided in the treatment of Bartter syndrome due to their potential to exacerbate metabolic alkalosis: While ACE inhibitors can lead to metabolic alkalosis, they are not contraindicated in the treatment of Bartter syndrome. The potential for metabolic alkalosis can be managed with careful monitoring of electrolyte levels and adjusting the dose of ACE inhibitors as necessary. @Neet_pg_bot

Kidneys also produce important hormones like vitamin D, erythropoietin, etc. This patient is suffering from metabolic acidosis with an increased anion gap. This metabolic acidosis results from the accumulation of organic acids in the body. Some of the causes of renal failure are diabetes, high blood pressure, chronic NSAID users, etc. The accumulation of organic acids is the main reason for the increased anion gap. questions.stem: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male patient presented in the outpatient department with complaints of fatigue and muscle weakness. The laboratory results revealed low pH, decreased bicarbonate ions, and high potassium. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type 4 is made. Which of the following is the cause of the above-mentioned patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hypoaldosteronism: Hypoaldosteronism is a condition in which there is a deficiency of aldosterone. Normally the activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system leads to the activation of aldosterone. The collecting duct of the nephron is the main site where the aldosterone acts. Normally aldosterone causes the excretion of hydrogen and potassium ions. However, in renal tubular acidosis type 4, there is a deficiency of aldosterone or aldosterone resistance, which results in hyperkalemia. Hyperkalemia can be fatal to the heart and can result in life-threatening arrhythmias. With hyperkalemia, ECG changes can occur. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hyperaldosteronism: Hyperaldosteronism is the excessive aldosterone production that results in excessive excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions. As a result, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis is seen in such patients. Option C - ADH deficiency: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) acts on vasopressin receptors that cause the expression of receptors in the distal part of nephrons causing the reabsorption of water. In ADH deficiency, there is insufficient ADH which results in excessive excretion of water leading to decreased urine osmolality and high serum osmolarity. Option D - SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone is a condition in which there is excessive retention of water due to excess ADH. The urine osmolality is high and there is hypervolemia. Some of the causes of SIADH are meningitis, encephalitis, brain tumors, psychosis, lung disease, etc. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 7-year-old child from a malaria-endemic region presents with profound fatigue, pallor, and abdominal discomfort. Physical examination reveals massive splenomegaly. Laboratory tests show anemia, jaundice, and elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH). The patient has had recurrent episodes of fever in the Past. questions.solution: Correct Option B - Kala Azar/Leishmaniasis: The symptoms described - profound fatigue, pallor, abdominal discomfort, massive splenomegaly, anemia, jaundice, elevated levels of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and recurrent episodes of fever - are characteristic of visceral leishmaniasis, also known as kala-azar. Kala-azar is caused by infection with the protozoan parasite Leishmania donovani. The infection is transmitted through the bite of infected sandflies. It is characterized by symptoms like fever, profound fatigue, anemia, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, and hyperpigmentation. Elevated LDH levels are also seen due to increased cell turnover. This condition is endemic in certain regions, including parts of Africa, Asia, and South America. Incorrect Options: Option A - Thalassemia Major: Thalassemia major is a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal hemoglobin production, leading to chronic anemia. While anemia is a common feature, other symptoms like fever, splenomegaly, and jaundice are not typical of thalassemia major. Option C - Mycobacterium Avium Complex: Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) is a group of bacteria that can cause infections, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems. It is not associated with the symptoms described in the scenario, such as anemia, splenomegaly, and jaundice. Option D - Felty Syndrome: Felty syndrome is a rare complication of rheumatoid arthritis (RA) characterized by the triad of RA, splenomegaly, and neutropenia. While it can cause splenomegaly, the other symptoms like profound fatigue, anemia, and jaundice are not typically associated with Felty syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B- Weight loss and lifestyle modification: The patient's clinical presentation, including loud snoring, witnessed apneas, excessive daytime sleepiness, and a high BMI, is suggestive of Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA). In patients with OSA, addressing modifiable risk factors is essential. Weight loss and lifestyle modification, such as positional therapy and avoidance of alcohol and sedative medications, are important first-line interventions. These measures can help reduce the severity of OSA and improve symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A- Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP): While CPAP is an effective treatment for moderate to severe OSA, initial management should focus on addressing modifiable risk factors. However, in this patient with a BMI of 32 and significant symptoms, lifestyle modifications should be the initial approach. Option D- Pharmacotherapy with modafinil: Modafinil is a wakefulness-promoting agent and is not a primary treatment for OSA. It may be considered in some cases to alleviate symptoms of excessive daytime sleepiness, but addressing underlying risk factors remains a priority. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Initiate memantine as an adjunct to donepezil: Memantine, an N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonist, is indicated as an adjunctive therapy to cholinesterase inhibitors, such as donepezil, in moderate to severe Alzheimer's disease. This combination provides a dual mechanism of action by targeting both the cholinergic and glutamatergic systems, offering a more comprehensive approach to symptom management. Incorrect Options: Option B - Increase the dose of donepezil: Increasing the dose of donepezil beyond the standard dosage is unlikely to provide additional cognitive benefits and may increase the risk of side effects. Option C - Prescribe rivastigmine for additional cholinesterase inhibition: Rivastigmine is another cholinesterase inhibitor, and adding it to the current regimen may lead to excessive cholinergic stimulation without significant additional benefits. Option D - Start high-dose vitamin E supplementation: High-dose vitamin E supplementation has not shown consistent efficacy in slowing cognitive decline in AD, and there are concerns about potential adverse effects at high doses. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C - Lobectomy In this case, the patient has a 1 cm thyroid nodule that has been confirmed to be papillary thyroid cancer through biopsy. Furthermore, the lesion is abutting the trachea, which raises concerns about its proximity to important structures in the neck. Given the size of the lesion and its location, a lobectomy is an appropriate treatment choice. A lobectomy involves the removal of one lobe of the thyroid gland (either the right or left) and is often the initial surgical treatment for small, localized thyroid cancers. It helps ensure complete removal of the cancer while preserving thyroid function. Incorrect Options: Option A - Active surveillance with serial ultrasound: Active surveillance is an option for small thyroid nodules with indeterminate characteristics, especially when they are less than 1 cm in size and do not exhibit concerning features on ultrasound. However, in this case, the lesion has been confirmed as papillary thyroid cancer, which is a malignant tumor. Active surveillance is not appropriate for known thyroid cancer because the goal is to remove the cancer and prevent its spread. Option B - Repeat biopsy to rule out other processes: Since the biopsy has already confirmed the presence of papillary thyroid cancer, repeating the biopsy is unlikely to change the diagnosis. The management should focus on treating the confirmed cancer rather than seeking further confirmation. Option D - Total thyroidectomy: Total thyroidectomy involves the complete removal of the thyroid gland. While this may be necessary in some cases of thyroid cancer, it is often reserved for larger tumors, more aggressive types of thyroid cancer, or cases where there is evidence of cancer spreading beyond the thyroid gland. In this case, a lobectomy is more appropriate, as the cancer is small, localized, and has not shown evidence of local adenopathy or distant spread. @Neet_pg_bot

Pain is limited to the anterior chest and is pleuritic and positional, worsening in the recumbent position. There is a history of recent self-limiting gastroenteritis 1 week back. Examination reveals normal vital signs with a pericardial friction rub at the left sternal border. ECG shows diffuse ST-elevation with reciprocal depression in lead aVR and V1. CRP and WBC count are raised. She has no history of such an event in the past. Considering the likely possibility, which of the following drug should be started?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Colchicine: The clinical scenario and physical findings are classical of acute pericarditis secondary to viral infection, and the drug of choice for this pregnant lady is colchicine. Acute viral or idiopathic pericarditis is a self-limiting disease of the pericardium. Non-specific and only symptomatic treatment are all that is needed for medical management of uncomplicated pericardial effusion. The first line drug in acute idiopathic or viral pericarditis includes nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), i.e. aspirin or ibuprofen with or without colchicine. NSAIDs are contraindicated in pregnancy, especially in the last trimester, as is this lady, therefore the first-line treatment option for this lady is to start with colchicine. Colchicine should be continued for 3 months at a dose of 0.5mg-0.6mg orally twice daily for individuals with >70kg weight and once daily for individuals with <70kg weight. Colchicine blocks the assembly of microtubules in WBCs, thereby exerting its anti-inflammatory effects. Colchicine, especially when used with NSAIDs, is well tolerated, alleviates symptoms and decreases the incidence of recurrence. Colchicine is not approved for pyogenic and malignancy-related pericarditis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Ibuprofen: Ibuprofen is not the right agent here as it is contraindicated in pregnancy of >20 weeks. Although NSAIDs are the first-line agent for treating idiopathic and viral pericarditis but are not safe in pregnancy. These can cause oligohydramnios and patent ductus arteriosus. Option C - Prednisolone: Prednisolone is not the right option to start with in this patient. Steroids are indicated for treating recurrent pericarditis or initial-treatment failure with NSAIDs or colchicine. As this patient presents with the first episode of pericarditis with no previous treatment exposure, this is not the right drug to start. Option D - Acyclovir: Acyclovir is not the right treatment for this patient. Antiviral therapy is not recommended for treating viral pericarditis as it is a self-limiting disease. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient has difficulty breathing and is diaphoretic. His vital signs are stable. Physical examination shows no acute findings. An ECG reveals the results shown below. Which vessel is most likely occluded in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 66-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension presents to the emergency department complaining of sudden-onset substernal chest pain that began while he was mowing his lawn 50 minutes ago. The patient has difficulty breathing and is diaphoretic. His vital signs are stable. Physical examination shows no acute findings. An ECG reveals the results shown below. Which vessel is most likely occluded in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - First diagonal branch of LAD: This patient has a high lateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), presenting to the emergency department in acute distress with sudden-onset chest pain during activity. Other symptoms such as diaphoresis and shortness of breath help narrow the suspicion to myocardial infarction. The ECG shows ST elevation in leads I and aVL, which are highly specific for a high lateral myocardial infarction. Reciprocal ST depression and T-wave inversion in both main inferior leads (Leads lll and aVF) are common findings due to the direction of depolarization occurring in those leads. The most common vessels occluded in a high lateral myocardial infarction are the first diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery or, less commonly, the obtuse marginal branch of the left circumflex artery. Incorrect Options: Option A - Left coronary artery: The left coronary artery (LCA) covers a wide range of myocardial tissue. Ischemia or infarct in LCA territory would show ST-segment changes in leads l, ll, and V4-V6. Reciprocal changes may appear in aVR. These changes are not observed in this patient’s ECG. Option C - Right coronary artery: The right coronary artery (RCA) mainly supplies the SA node and the inferior aspect of the heart. It gives off the posterior descending artery in most of the population. Occlusion of the RCA would show ST-segment changes most commonly in leads ll, lll, and aVF. Option D - Posterior descending artery: The posterior descending artery (PDA) mainly supplies the AV node, posterior third of the interventricular septum, posteromedial papillary muscle, and posterior two-thirds of the ventricular wall. Findings on this ECG do not indicate a PDA occlusion, which would usually show ST-segment depression in leads V1-V4. If posterior leads were added, ST elevation would manifest in leads V7-V9. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B
options.text: Decreases overall rates of prostate cancer, with slightly improved overall survival

questions.answerText: Decreases overall rates of prostate cancer, with slightly increased risk of high grade prostate cancer
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Decreases overall rates of prostate cancer, with slightly increased risk of high grade prostate cancer: In the Prostate Cancer Prevention Trial (PCPT, Thompson et al, NEJM, 2003), ~19,000 men at elevated risk for prostate cancer ( age >= 55, African-American ethnicity, or first degree relative with prostate cancer) were randomized to placebo or finasteride (5 mg/day). There was a statistically significant decrease incidence of prostate cancer in men assigned to finasteride compared to placebo (10.5% vs 14.9%). There was a small, but statistically significant increase in the risk of high-grade prostate cancer (GS >= 7) with finasteride (3.5% vs 3.0%, p=0.05). 15-year overall survival rates (OS) were similar (~73-74%) in both arms. At a median 16 years of follow-up, finasteride maintained a 21% reduction in the risk of prostate cancer, but the protective effect was only significant through 7.5 years. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increases overall rates of prostate cancer, with decreased overall survival: This option is not accurate. Finasteride is not known to increase the overall rates of prostate cancer. In fact, its primary use in the context of prostate cancer is to reduce the risk of developing the disease. There's no strong evidence suggesting a significant improvement in overall survival due to finasteride use. Option D - No change in rates of prostate cancer: This option is not accurate. Finasteride has been shown to decrease the overall rates of prostate cancer, especially low-grade cancers. However, there is a small increased risk of high-grade prostate cancer as mentioned earlier. @Neet_pg_bot

While the development of cGVHD is influenced by various factors, including the patient's underlying disease, the conditioning regimen, and the immune system's interaction between the donor and recipient, there is no known direct correlation between the sex (gender) of the donor and recipient and the risk of cGVHD. Option D - Peripheral blood stem cell rather than bone marrow or umbilical cord: The source of stem cells can influence the risk of cGVHD. 	No growth on extended culture (6 weeks)

Which of the following would be recommended for treating his persistent arthropathy?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Hydroxychloroquine: Lyme disease is caused by infection with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi. Patients often develop an arthropathy that starts as a flitting arthropathy but then develops into a large joint monoarthropathy often in the wrist, knee, or ankle. It may become chronic in around 10% of patients with the majority of these cases affecting the knee. If the arthropathy does not resolve after two courses of antibiotics it can be helpful to introduce Hydroxychloroquine. Incorrect Options: Option B - Methotrexate: It is an immunosuppressive medication commonly used to treat autoimmune diseases like rheumatoid arthritis. Lyme arthritis is an infectious process caused by the bacterium Borrelia burgdorferi, and the recommended approach is to ensure that the infection has been completely treated before considering immunosuppressive medications. In this case, the joint fluid analysis and culture results do not suggest ongoing infection, so focusing on immune modulation would be more appropriate. Option C - Mycophenolate Mofetil: It is another immunosuppressive medication used to treat various autoimmune diseases. Like methotrexate, its use in cases of persistent joint symptoms following Lyme disease would likely be considered only if the infection has been fully ruled out. Option D - Penicillamine: A chelating agent that has been used in the past for certain autoimmune conditions, but its use has decreased due to potential side effects. It is not a common or recommended treatment for persistent joint symptoms following Lyme disease. The focus should be on addressing the underlying cause of the joint symptoms rather than using chelating agents. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 28-year-old male who presented with mild chest pain, cough, and the subjective feeling of shortness of breath was evaluated, and found to have an anterior mediastinal mass with no additional lesion concerns for metastatic spread in his CT thorax. His AFP level was normal and beta-hCG level was 488 IU/L. Based on the patient's clinical presentation, which of the following treatments would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male who presented with mild chest pain, cough, and the subjective feeling of shortness of breath was evaluated, and found to have an anterior mediastinal mass with no additional lesion concerns for metastatic spread in his CT thorax. His AFP level was normal and beta-hCG level was 488 IU/L. Based on the patient's clinical presentation, which of the following treatments would you recommend?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Chemotherapy +/- surgery: Based on the clinical information above, his presentation is most consistent with a mediastinal seminoma without evidence of metastatic spread. Mediastinal germ cell tumour are generally managed with chemotherapy followed by surgical resection. Mediastinal seminoma without metastases is considered Good-Risk and chemotherapy consists of 3 cycles of bleomycin, cisplatin, and etoposide (BEP) or 4 cycles of EP chemotherapy. Like testicular and CNS seminoma, mediastinal seminomas are quite sensitive to chemotherapy and thus surgery is generally considered for residual disease after chemotherapy. Note that not all cases of residual disease after chemotherapy should have surgery, and the management of residual mass after chemotherapy is controversial. These patients should be managed in a multidisciplinary setting. Using this treatment paradigm the long term overall survival rate is excellent. For patients that are unable to tolerate chemotherapy, radiation therapy can be considered, as seminomas are also responsive to radiation. Note that all mediastinal non-seminoma germ cell tumors (NSGCT) are Poor-Risk and should be treated with 4 cycles of BEP or 4 cycles of VIP (Etoposide, Ifosfamide plus Mesna, and Cisplatin). Incorrect Options: Option A - Surgery alone: Surgery alone is not recommended in this case. While surgery might be an option for localized testicular tumors, an anterior mediastinal mass with elevated serum markers suggests a non-seminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT), which is more aggressive and usually requires a multimodal approach involving chemotherapy and potentially surgery. Option B - Surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy: This option could be considered, but it's important to note that chemotherapy is typically administered before surgery in the management of NSGCT. Chemotherapy helps to shrink the tumor and treat any potential microscopic spread of the disease. Option C - Surgery + adjuvant radiation: Radiation therapy is not typically used as the primary treatment for non-seminomatous germ cell tumors. Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment, and radiation might be considered in specific cases, usually after surgery, for residual masses that are resistant to chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 75-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital for respiratory distress and is treated for influenza. After 5 days of treatment, he continues to have a fever. On day 8, the nurse inquires about removing droplet precautions. What is the most appropriate course of action?
questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old patient is admitted to the hospital for respiratory distress and is treated for influenza. After 5 days of treatment, he continues to have a fever. On day 8, the nurse inquires about removing droplet precautions. What is the most appropriate course of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved

options.label: B
options.text: Discontinue droplet precautions since the patient finished treatment

options.label: C
options.text: Relocate the patient to a negative-pressure room

questions.answerText: Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Continue droplet precautions until the fever is resolved Influenza is predominantly transmitted via droplets. The virus is shed from the airway and spread by coughing and sneezing. Other ways of transmission are of lesser importance. Shedding of the virus may continue despite treatment. The current recommendation indicates that droplet precautions can be dropped after 7 days from the onset of the illness or 24 hours after resolution of the symptoms (whichever is longer). In this particular example, the patient experienced a fever, so isolation precaution should be continued. Incorrect Options: Option B - Discontinue droplet precautions since the patient finished treatment: This option is incorrect because the patient still has a fever after 5 days of influenza treatment. Even though the patient completed the treatment course, the persistence of the fever suggests that the infection may not have completely resolved. Droplet precautions should be continued until the fever has resolved to prevent the potential spread of the infection to others. Option C - Relocate the patient to a negative-pressure room: This option is also incorrect. Negative-pressure rooms are typically used for patients with airborne infections, such as tuberculosis or measles, where the infectious particles can remain suspended in the air for an extended period. Influenza is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets, not through the airborne route. Thus, relocating the patient to a negative-pressure room is not necessary in this case. Option D - Repeat treatment with Tamiflu: This option is incorrect because it assumes that the patient's fever is persisting due to an inadequate response to the initial Tamiflu treatment. However, it's important to note that some patients with influenza, especially elderly individuals or those with compromised immune systems, may experience a prolonged fever even after appropriate antiviral treatment. Repeating Tamiflu without any clinical indication may not be necessary and could lead to potential side effects without any significant benefit. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following parasitic infections is usually associated with occult blood in stool?
questions.solution: Correct Option D- Strongyloides: TRUE: Occult blood in stool is associated with hookworm or Strongyloides infection. Strongyloides stercoralis enters the human host when skin contacts the larvae through infected soil usually contaminated with feces. questions.solution: Correct Option A - Oral contraceptive pills: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia (CAH) is a genetic condition marked by impaired steroid hormone synthesis in the adrenal glands. As a result, there is an increase in the production of androgens and the accumulation of their precursors, which can cause female virilization. Most commonly, glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids are used in hormone replacement therapy to treat CAH by replacing the missing hormones. Though some CAH patients may still experience elevated androgen levels and hyperandrogenism-related symptoms, like excessive hair growth, irregular menses, even with adequate hormone replacement, this is not always the case. The best course of action in this situation for the patient's symptoms would be oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) secretion from the pituitary gland. OCPs contain estrogen and progesterone, which can inhibit the hypothalamic release of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) and the pituitary gland's subsequent release of luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). This may lead to a reduction in ovarian androgen production as well as a reduction in peripheral androgen activation. OCPs can therefore successfully lower androgen levels and ameliorate the symptoms of hyperandrogenism in females with CAH. Parathyroid hormone acts on the different parts of the body, which causes the serum calcium levels to increase and serum phosphate levels to decrease in the following ways: Bones It stimulates the osteoblasts at a low serum level, thus building bone. options.label: C

options.label: D

questions.solution: Correct Option A - Decreasing the physiologic dead space: The total quantities of the alveoli that are not involved in gas exchange and the air volume in the conducting passageways make up the physiologic dead space. (i.e., alveolar dead space). The disparity between minute ventilation (tidal volume x breathing rate) and alveolar ventilation is decreased by reducing the metabolic dead space ([tidal volume – physiologic dead space volume] x respiratory rate). Physiologic dead space in sound lungs is comparable to physical dead space. There is greater alveolar space ventilation in illnesses (like pulmonary embolism) that cause reduced lung tissue perfusion. Pathological conditions that can increase the physiological dead space are as follows. Pulmonary embolism Emphysema Acute respiratory distress syndrome COPD Incorrect Options: Option B - Increasing the respiratory rate: Increasing the breathing rate improves both minute ventilation and lung ventilation. However, the amount of the rise in minute ventilation is higher than that of alveolar ventilation because increased respiratory rate also raises alveolar dead space ventilation. As a result, raising the respiratory rate increases, not reducing the disparity between a minute and alveolar ventilation. Option C - Increasing the partial pressure of inhaled oxygen: Increasing the partial pressure of breathed oxygen enhances blood circulation by raising the alveolar partial pressure of oxygen. Because gas travels from regions of high partial pressure to areas of low partial pressure, a larger pressure differential produces a powerful gradient for oxygen to diffuse across the blood-air barrier into the blood. The partial pressure of breathed oxygen does not affect breathing or volume metrics. Option D - Decreasing the affinity of hemoglobin for oxygen: It is easier for oxygen to be released into distal tissues, which improves tissue oxygenation when hemoglobin's preference for oxygen is reduced (i.e., the oxygen dissociation curve for hemoglobin is shifted to the right). Ventilation or capacity factors are unaffected. @Neet_pg_bot

These symptoms eventually went away after his team camped in the same location for an extra day. He is otherwise healthy, and his examination is completely unremarkable. The patient has no past medical history of concern. Which of the following is the best recommendation to avoid or prevent these symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old male presents to your OPD. He is seeking a regular physical examination as well as a consultation regarding dizziness and headaches he experienced the last time he ascended a mountain. options.label: A
options.text: No further climbing due to life-threatening illness risk last time

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Acetazolamide: The most appropriate preventive measure for acute mountain sickness for this patient is acetazolamide. Acute mountain sickness (AMS) generally occurs at >2500 meters; however, it has been reported at lower altitudes. AMS is a syndrome of nonspecific manifestations that can develop within 6-12 hours. Patients experience headaches, dizziness, fatigue, and/or nausea with little to no physical exam findings. The most prominent risk factors for developing altitude illness are a history of altitude illness and the rate of ascent. Why this occurs is still unknown, but MR studies suggest that vasogenic cerebral edema is a component of high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE), which is on a spectrum with AMS. The prevention and treatment of AMS include a gradual ascent allowing acclimation, which is how this patient had a resolution of his symptoms on his prior climb. There is thought to be individual variation, but a graded ascent of at most 400 meters above 3000 meters is recommended. Another measure that is thought to be protective is exposure to high altitudes within 2 months of the intended climb, which may lower rates of AMS by 50%. Hydration is important in preventing dehydration secondary to insensible losses (sweating hyperventilation). In regards to pharmacological prevention of AMS, acetazolamide is the drug of choice. Acetazolamide inhibits renal carbonic anhydrase, causing bicarbonate diuresis with subsequent metabolic acidosis and hyperventilation with a relative risk reduction of 48% vs. placebo. Incorrect Options: Option A - No further climbing due to life-threatening illness risk last time: The patient's symptoms of dizziness and headaches during mountain climbing are likely due to acute mountain sickness (AMS), which is not a life-threatening condition. However, any indication of high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) or high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE), which are more severe forms of altitude illness, would require immediate descent due to the potential life-threatening nature of these conditions. Option C - Ginkgo biloba: Ginkgo biloba has not been shown to be effective in the prevention of acute mountain sickness (AMS). The most effective pharmacological prevention for AMS is acetazolamide. Option D - Spironolactone: Spironolactone is not used for the prevention of acute mountain sickness (AMS). Acetazolamide is the drug of choice for pharmacological prevention of AMS. @Neet_pg_bot

Which of the following drugs is commonly used in the treatment of CKD to reduce proteinuria?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Lisinopril Lisinopril is an angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitor medication that is commonly used in the treatment of CKD. It acts by blocking the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. By inhibiting angiotensin II, lisinopril reduces aldosterone secretion and promotes sodium and water excretion, which can lead to hyperkalemia. Angiotensin II specifically constrict the efferent arteriole and increases the glomerular filtration pressure, and increases the proteinuria. One of the therapeutic effects of ACE inhibitors is reducing proteinuria by dilating the efferent arteriole and thus decreasing the filtration pressure, which ultimately leads to reduced proteinuria, which is a common complication of CKD. Incorrect options: Option B: Hydrochlorothiazide Hydrochlorothiazide is a thiazide diuretic medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It decreases sodium reabsorption and therefore decreases fluid reabsorption; this directly causes decreased levels of circulating sodium. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option C: Amlodipine Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker medication that can help reduce blood pressure in patients with hypertension and CKD. It does not have a significant effect on reducing proteinuria. Option D: Spironolactone Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic medication that can also reduce blood pressure in patients with CKD. It has no effect on reducing proteinuria. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following theories of aging in geriatric medicine suggests that aging is primarily driven by the accumulation of DNA damage and mutations over time?

questions.stem: Which of the following interventions/factors has NOT been proven to influence the risk of developing a post-lumbar puncture headache?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following interventions/factors has NOT been proven to influence the risk of developing a post-lumbar puncture headache?

options.label: C
options.text: Replacement of the stylet prior to removal of the needle

options.label: D
options.text: Bevel orientation of a Quincke needle

questions.solution: Correct Option B - Bedrest post-procedure: Despite the common practice of recommending bedrest (“lying flat’) for 30-60 minutes post-procedure, option B is the only factor/intervention of the options listed that hasn’t been shown to have any association with reducing the incidence of post-dural puncture headache (PDPH). Similarly, many of the other factors commonly felt to be associated with an increased risk of a PDPH including patient position, the volume of CSF removed, and the number of attempts made, have also been shown to have no influence on the risk of PDPH. Incorrect Options: Option A - Use of an atraumatic needle: Atraumatic needles, such as Sprotte or Whitacre needles, have a lower risk of causing post-lumbar puncture headaches compared to traditional cutting needles (e.g., Quincke needle). These needles have a rounded tip that separates rather than cuts the dural fibers, reducing the risk of CSF leakage and subsequent headaches. Option C - Replacement of the stylet prior to removal of the needle: Removing the stylet (the inner part of the needle) before removing the needle can create a temporary seal at the puncture site, reducing the risk of CSF leakage and post-lumbar puncture headache. Option D - Bevel orientation of a Quincke needle: The bevel orientation of a Quincke needle (cutting needle) can influence the risk of post-lumbar puncture headache. The bevel orientation should be parallel to the longitudinal axis of the spinal cord, as this reduces the risk of dural fibers being cut and CSF leakage. Option E - Use of a higher gauge (≥ 20 G) needle for the procedure: Smaller gauge needles (e.g., 22 G or 25 G) have been associated with a lower risk of post-lumbar puncture headaches compared to larger gauge needles. The smaller needle size causes less trauma to the dura and reduces the likelihood of CSF leakage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: The 69-year-old gentleman presents to the emergency room with a growing neck mass, biopsy from the right-sided supraclavicular lymph node revealed a poorly differentiated carcinoma. CT scan of the chest and neck is otherwise unremarkable. It does stain for TTF-1. Which 2 primary sites of disease does this narrow the differential down to?
questions.stemHtml: The 69-year-old gentleman presents to the emergency room with a growing neck mass, biopsy from the right-sided supraclavicular lymph node revealed a poorly differentiated carcinoma. CT scan of the chest and neck is otherwise unremarkable. It does stain for TTF-1. Which 2 primary sites of disease does this narrow the differential down to?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Lung and thyroid: The presence of TTF-1 (Thyroid Transcription Factor-1) staining in a poorly differentiated carcinoma from a supraclavicular lymph node biopsy narrows down the likely primary sites of disease to the lung and thyroid. TTF-1 Staining : TTF-1 is a nuclear protein that is often expressed in cells originating from the thyroid gland and the lungs. It is a valuable immunohistochemical marker for identifying the primary site of certain carcinomas, especially poorly differentiated ones. Lung and Thyroid : TTF-1 staining is commonly associated with primary lung adenocarcinomas and primary thyroid carcinomas. Therefore, the presence of TTF-1 staining in the biopsy specimen suggests that the poorly differentiated carcinoma could originate from either the lung or the thyroid. Incorrect Options: Option B - Thyroid Only: While TTF-1 staining is frequently seen in thyroid carcinomas, it is not exclusive to the thyroid. The presence of TTF-1 staining alone does not rule out the possibility of lung involvement. Therefore, this option is too restrictive. Option C - Lung Only: TTF-1 staining is indeed associated with lung adenocarcinomas, but it can also be present in thyroid carcinomas. As a result, it is not specific enough to definitively conclude that the primary site is only the lung. Option D - Lung, Thyroid, and Head & Neck: While TTF-1 staining can occasionally be seen in some head and neck cancers, it is not commonly associated with this site of origin. Therefore, including head and neck as a primary site in the differential diagnosis is less likely in the presence of TTF-1 staining. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A- Neural crest cells: The aortic root is derived from the neural crest cells . Neural crest cells migrate from the neural tube and form the aorticopulmonary septum . The aorticopulmonary septum divides the truncus arteriosus into the aorta and pulmonary trunk. The aortic root includes the aortic valve, Valsalva sinuses, and the ascending aorta's beginning. Incorrect Options: Option B- Splanchnic mesoderm: The splanchnic mesoderm gives rise to the cardiovascular system, including the heart tube and major blood vessels. Option C- Intermediate mesoderm: The intermediate mesoderm gives rise to the urogenital system . Option D-Surface ectoderm: The surface ectoderm gives rise to the skin, hair, nails, and glands. @Neet_pg_bot

He has been on hemodialysis for the past six months and has a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2. Which of the following is the most appropriate indication for renal transplantation in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with end-stage renal disease due to polycystic kidney disease has presented to the physician's clinic. He has been on hemodialysis for the past six months and has a history of hypertension and diabetes mellitus type 2. Which of the following is the most appropriate indication for renal transplantation in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C- Symptomatic uremia: Patients with end-stage renal disease (Irreversible kidney dysfunction with eGFR < 15 mL/min/1.73 m2) often experience a range of symptoms due to the accumulation of waste products and the loss of kidney function. These symptoms, collectively known as uremia, can include fatigue, nausea, vomiting, pericarditis, peripheral neuropathy pleuritis, lethargy, confusion, seizures, somnolence, coma, and pruritus. There is increased bleeding risk and infection. Renal transplantation is a well-established treatment for uremia , as it can restore kidney function and alleviate these symptoms. Incorrect Options: Option A- Uncontrolled hypertension: Although hypertension is a common complication of end-stage renal disease, it does not indicate renal transplantation. Hypertension can usually be managed with medications and lifestyle changes, and kidney transplantation may not necessarily improve hypertension control. Option B- Poor glycemic control: While diabetes mellitus is a common cause of end-stage renal disease, poor glycemic control does not indicate renal transplantation. Transplantation may improve glucose control in some patients, but other treatments can also achieve glycemic control . Option D- Polycystic kidney disease: Polycystic kidney disease (PKD) is a genetic disorder that causes cysts to form in the kidneys, leading to progressive kidney damage and end-stage renal disease. PKD is a common indication for renal transplantation, as it is usually irreversible and can only be treated by replacing the damaged kidneys with a healthy donor kidney. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 75-year-old man presents to the pulmonology clinic with a complaint of difficulty to breath and coughing. The patient has a 40-pack-year smoking history. On examination, the patient has a pink appearance and is cachectic with obvious difficulty breathing with pursed lips. The post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC ratio is 0.6. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Emphysema COPD is the persistent airflow limitation caused by obstruction of smaller airways and limitation of airflow in which FEV1/FVC < 0.70 is characteristic. Emphysema is a type of COPD characterised by the loss of alveoli due to the destruction of alveolar walls and capillaries, which result in permanent dilatation of pulmonary airspaces. These patients are cachectic with a pink appearance because the partial pressure of oxygen is not much reduced. Incorrect Options: Option A - Asthma Asthma is a chronic respiratory inflammatory disease characterised by bronchial hypersensitivity and reversible airflow obstruction. Patients present with severe shortness of breath, cough and wheezing. It may be allergic asthma due to triggers such as atopy, pollen, domestic animals, mites, mould spores and floor dust. Non-allergic asthma is due to viral respiratory tract infection, cold air, exercise-induced asthma, stress, and aspirin-induced asthma. Option C - Chronic bronchitis Chronic bronchitis is a type of COPD characterised by chronic cough with expectoration for at least three months per year for two consecutive years. A productive cough is the hallmark of the disease rather than shortness of breath. Patients are obese and have central cyanosis due to hypoxia and may also have peripheral oedema. Therefore, these patients are called “blue bloaters.” Option D - Bronchiectasis Bronchiectasis is an abnormal and irreversible dilatation of the bronchial tree due to progressive obstruction of the airway and mucous plugging by repeated bronchial inflammation. It may be caused by cystic fibrosis or after severe pneumonia, primary ciliary dyskinesia, Kartagener syndrome and allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, smoking and bronchial narrowing by COPD. Patients present with copious mucopurulent sputum, repeated rhinosinusitis, and blood in sputum. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which two factors are used to determine median overall survival in the multiple myeloma International Staging System(ISS)?
questions.stemHtml: Which two factors are used to determine median overall survival in the multiple myeloma International Staging System(ISS)?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Beta-2 microglobulin and Albumin: The ISS for multiple myeloma is a widely used staging system that relies on just two factors to determine prognosis: beta-2 microglobulin and albumin. Beta-2 microglobulin is a marker of tumor burden and is associated with poor prognosis when elevated. Albumin, on the other hand, is a marker of overall health and nutrition, and low levels are associated with worse outcomes. The combination of these two factors allows for a relatively simple and effective way to stratify patients into different prognostic groups. Incorrect Options: Option B - PTT and Bilirubin: Neither partial thromboplastin time (PTT) nor bilirubin is used in the ISS for multiple myeloma staging. These factors are not typically associated with the staging of multiple myeloma. Option C - Calcium and INR: While hypercalcemia (elevated calcium levels) can be seen in multiple myeloma and is an important clinical feature, it is not one of the factors used in the ISS staging system. INR (International Normalized Ratio) is a measure of blood clotting and is not a component of the ISS. Option D - M-protein and LDH: M-protein (monoclonal protein) is a key marker in the diagnosis and monitoring of multiple myeloma, but it is not used in the ISS for staging. LDH (lactate dehydrogenase) is an enzyme that can be elevated in various conditions, including some malignancies, but it is not a component of the ISS staging system. @Neet_pg_bot
