questions.answerText: In addition to blood clots, patients may present with livedo reticularis
questions.solution: Correct Option D - In addition to blood clots, patients may present with livedo reticularis: In addition to blood clots, patients with antiphospholipid antibody syndrome may present with livedo reticularis. Livedo reticularis is a condition characterized by a mottled or net-like pattern of reddish or bluish discoloration of the skin. It is often seen in patients with antiphospholipid syndrome and can be associated with the vascular changes caused by the syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option A - Antiphospholipid syndrome only occurs concurrently with another autoimmune disorder: While antiphospholipid is seen more frequently in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) than in the general population -- and can be associated with other autoimmune diseases -- it can also occur as an isolated condition. Option B - If the diagnosis is confirmed, the patient’s immediate family members should be tested for antiphospholipid antibodies and, if positive, anticoagulated: The presence of an antiphospholipid antibody in of itself is not an indication for anticoagulation. Anticoagulation is indicated for patients with antiphospholipid antibodies who have experienced a blood clot. For such patients, lifelong anticoagulation is recommended. Given the current lack of evidence, warfarin should be used over the new generation of anticoagulants. Option C - Her obstetrician should have started anticoagulation after the patient had multiple miscarriages: In patients with obstetric antiphospholipid syndrome -- that is, women diagnosed based upon antibody titers and obstetric complications without a prior blood clot -- there is inadequate data to recommend anticoagulation to prevent the occurrence of the first thrombosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male presents with complaints of headache, lethargy, and nausea for the last 20 days after an episode of pneumonia. On examination, there is no remarkable finding but laboratory investigations reveal a serum sodium level of 128mEq/L, serum osmolality 270mOsm/kg, urinary sodium level of 44mEq/L, and urinary osmolality 110mOsm/kg. What is the first-line treatment for a mild case of this disease?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male presents with complaints of headache, lethargy, and nausea for the last 20 days after an episode of pneumonia. On examination, there is no remarkable finding but laboratory investigations reveal a serum sodium level of 128mEq/L, serum osmolality 270mOsm/kg, urinary sodium level of 44mEq/L, and urinary osmolality 110mOsm/kg. What is the first-line treatment for a mild case of this disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Fluid restriction: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excess ADH secretion which causes excess water absorption from the kidney and results in concentrated urine SIADH is diagnosed by Serum sodium lower than 135mEq/L Serum osmolality lower than 275mOsm/kg Urine sodium higher than 40mEq/L Urine osmolality higher than 100mOsm/kg With normal blood pressure and euvolemia and no other causes of hyponatremia Pulmonary diseases like pneumonia, asthma, acute respiratory failure, and pneumothorax can cause SIADH due to unknown mechanism Clinical manifestations are due to decreased serum osmolality due to ADH-mediated water retention and secondary solute loss which causes cerebral edema The 1st line treatment for a patient with mild symptoms is the fluid restriction The daily water intake is restricted to less than 800ml only This restricted intake of water decreases free water in the body and increases serum osmolality and improves symptoms Incorrect Options: Option B - Salt tablets: If the 1st line treatment of water restriction is not helpful and hyponatremia is persistent then sodium chloride in the form of salt tablets can be given to correct hyponatremia Salt tablets cause effective and rapid response than water restriction Option C - Salt tablets with furosemide: Salt tablets (sodium chloride) can be used with furosemide (a loop diuretic) as it decreases the urine concentration and helps the excretion of water This is not a first-line treatment and is used after water restriction Option D - Hypertonic saline infusion: The hypertonic saline infusion will rapidly increase the serum sodium levels and will cause osmotic demyelination syndrome In a patient with mild symptoms of hyponatremia rapid correction with hypertonic saline is not recommended @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A - Fluid restriction:

  • Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH) is characterized by excess ADH secretion which causes excess water absorption from the kidney and results in concentrated urine
  • SIADH is diagnosed by
    • Serum sodium lower than 135mEq/L
    • Serum osmolality lower than 275mOsm/kg
    • Urine sodium higher than 40mEq/L
    • Urine osmolality higher than 100mOsm/kg
    • With normal blood pressure and euvolemia and no other causes of hyponatremia
  • Pulmonary diseases like pneumonia, asthma, acute respiratory failure, and pneumothorax can cause SIADH due to unknown mechanism
  • Clinical manifestations are due to decreased serum osmolality due to ADH-mediated water retention and secondary solute loss which causes cerebral edema
  • The 1st line treatment for a patient with mild symptoms is the fluid restriction
  • The daily water intake is restricted to less than 800ml only
  • This restricted intake of water decreases free water in the body and increases serum osmolality and improves symptoms

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Salt tablets:

  • If the 1st line treatment of water restriction is not helpful and hyponatremia is persistent then sodium chloride in the form of salt tablets can be given to correct hyponatremia
  • Salt tablets cause effective and rapid response than water restriction

Option C - Salt tablets with furosemide:

  • Salt tablets (sodium chloride) can be used with furosemide (a loop diuretic) as it decreases the urine concentration and helps the excretion of water
  • This is not a first-line treatment and is used after water restriction

Option D - Hypertonic saline infusion:

  • The hypertonic saline infusion will rapidly increase the serum sodium levels and will cause osmotic demyelination syndrome
  • In a patient with mild symptoms of hyponatremia rapid correction with hypertonic saline is not recommended

questions.answerText: Continue with same regimen in the adjuvant setting
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Continue with same regimen in the adjuvant setting : In this case: The patient received neoadjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin and doxorubicin. Surgical resection was performed with wide local excision, and the margins were negative (clear), indicating that there was no visible tumor at the surgical margins. However, the pathologic examination of the surgical specimen revealed that 25% of the tumor tissue was still viable. This means that a significant portion of the tumor did not respond completely to chemotherapy. The recommended course of action in such cases, where there is a partial response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy but clear surgical margins, is to continue with the same chemotherapy regimen in the adjuvant setting. Adjuvant chemotherapy is administered after surgery to eliminate any remaining cancer cells and reduce the risk of recurrence. Incorrect Options: Option A - Clinical and radiographic surveillance: Surveillance without further treatment may not be sufficient in this case, as there is evidence of viable tumor remaining in the surgical specimen. Option C - Radiation therapy: Radiation therapy is not typically the first-line treatment for osteosarcoma but may be considered in certain cases, such as when there is inadequate surgical margin control or when the tumor is unresectable. In this case, the patient already had clear surgical margins, and the standard approach is to continue with chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting. Option D - Sorafenib: Sorafenib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor used in the treatment of some cancers, but it is not a standard treatment for osteosarcoma. The recommended approach in this case is to continue with chemotherapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Beyond genetic testing, which of the following diagnostic tests is often used when considering a diagnosis of Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)?
questions.stemHtml: Beyond genetic testing, which of the following diagnostic tests is often used when considering a diagnosis of Cerebral Autosomal Dominant Arteriopathy with Subcortical Infarcts and Leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Skin biopsy: The diagnosis of CADASIL is made with the combination of clinical history, exam, MRI findings, skin biopsy and genetic testing. Although sequencing of the NOTCH3 gene is the gold standard diagnostic test, skin biopsy may also help make the diagnosis due to the involvement of systemic arterioles in addition to the central nervous system vasculature. Electron microscopy of the skin biopsy may show granular osmiophilic material near the basement membrane of arteriole smooth muscle cells. The use of NOTCH3 antibodies may increase the sensitivity of skin biopsy. The other choices have not been systematically assessed for diagnosis of CADASIL and are more invasive and higher risk than skin biopsy. Nonetheless, these changes are present in nerve and muscle tissue as well (see link below) and one could consider evaluating arterioles in these tissues in an individual suspected to have the illness if the tissue is already available for an alternative purpose. Incorrect Options: Option A - Liver biopsy: Liver biopsy is not used for the diagnosis of CADASIL. CADASIL primarily affects the brain and small blood vessels, and liver biopsy is not relevant to this condition. Option C - Muscle biopsy: Muscle biopsy is not a standard diagnostic test for CADASIL. The condition primarily involves the brain's small blood vessels, and muscle biopsy would not provide relevant information for this diagnosis. Option D - Nerve biopsy: Nerve biopsy is not routinely used for the diagnosis of CADASIL. The disease primarily affects the cerebral arteries and small blood vessels in the brain, and nerve biopsy is not a standard procedure for evaluating this condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following forms of thalassemia is typically not compatible with life?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following forms of thalassemia is typically not compatible with life?
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Alpha Thalassemia - Hemoglobin Barts: Hemoglobin Barts, also known as Hb Barts or γ4 tetramers, is a type of alpha thalassemia. It occurs when all four alpha-globin genes are deleted or severely mutated. This condition leads to the absence of functional alpha-globin chains, which are necessary for the production of normal adult hemoglobin (HbA). Fetuses affected by Hemoglobin Barts usually do not survive to term, and if they are born, they often die shortly after birth due to severe anemia and tissue hypoxia. The lack of functional alpha-globin chains results in the formation of gamma-globin tetramers (Hb Barts) that cannot adequately carry oxygen. This inability to transport oxygen contributes to the severe health issues associated with this condition. Incorrect Options: Option B - Alpha Thalassemia - Hemoglobin H Disease: Hemoglobin H disease results from the deletion of three alpha-globin genes, leaving only one functional alpha-globin gene. Individuals with Hemoglobin H disease can survive but often experience moderate to severe anemia and may require regular blood transfusions. Their life expectancy varies depending on the severity of the condition. Option C - Beta Thalassemia - Beta Thalassemia Major: Beta thalassemia major, also known as Cooley's anemia, is a severe form of beta thalassemia. It occurs when both beta-globin genes are mutated or absent, leading to the lack of functional beta-globin chains required to form HbA. Individuals with beta thalassemia major require lifelong blood transfusions and chelation therapy to manage iron overload resulting from frequent transfusions. With proper treatment, they can survive into adulthood, although the quality of life may be significantly impacted. Option D - Beta Thalassemia - Beta Thalassemia Intermedia: Beta thalassemia intermedia is a milder form of beta thalassemia. Individuals with beta thalassemia intermedia often require occasional or no blood transfusions, as they can produce some functional beta-globin chains. Life expectancy varies widely in this group, and individuals may experience moderate to severe symptoms but generally have a better prognosis compared to beta thalassemia major. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Bernard-Soulier syndrome: Bernard-Soulier syndrome is a rare congenital bleeding disorder characterized by thrombocytopenia (low platelet count) and giant platelets. It is caused by mutations in the GP1BA, GP1BB, or GP9 genes, which code for the glycoprotein Ib-IX-V complex on the platelet surface. This complex is responsible for platelet adhesion to the endothelium at sites of vascular injury. In Bernard-Soulier syndrome, the dysfunctional glycoprotein complex leads to impaired platelet adhesion, causing bleeding symptoms such as petechiae, easy bruising, and mucosal bleeding. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hemophilia A: Hemophilia A is a deficiency of factor VIII, a clotting factor. It does not involve thrombocytopenia or platelet dysfunction. Option B - von Willebrand disease: von Willebrand disease is characterized by deficiencies or defects in von Willebrand factor, which plays a role in platelet adhesion. However, it typically does not result in thrombocytopenia or giant platelets as seen in Bernard-Soulier syndrome. Option C - Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP): ITP is an autoimmune disorder characterized by isolated thrombocytopenia due to the destruction of platelets by autoantibodies. It does not involve genetic mutations like Bernard-Soulier syndrome does. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D- Autonomic dysfunction and aerophobia: Rabies encephalitis is characterized by progressive central nervous system involvement. Autonomic dysfunction, including fluctuations in blood pressure and heart rate, and aerophobia (fear of air or wind) are classic features of rabies. Hydrophobia, the inability to swallow water due to painful spasms of the pharyngeal muscles, is also a hallmark symptom. questions.solution: Correct Option B - A homonymous right superior quadrantanopia: The left optic radiations serving vision in the right hemifield (in both eyes) originate in the left lateral geniculate nucleus and project to the primary visual cortex in the occipital lobe. Fibers serving the superior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the left temporal lobe in a structure known as the loop of Meyer which passes anteriorly as far as approximately 2.5 cm from the tip of the temporal lobe. Fibers serving the inferior right quadrant of vision (in both eyes) project through the parietal lobe to the primary visual cortex. Lesions of the optic tracts classically cause incongruous (asymmetric between the two eyes) field defects because the visual pathway fibers serving corresponding points in space are not closely approximated. In other words, the more posterior the lesion of the retrochiasmal visual pathways, the more organized the visual pathways fibers are and the more congruous (or symmetric) the visual field defects tend to be. Indeed, occipital lobe lesions tend to cause very congruous homonymous field defects. Lesions of the optic tract anterior to the brachium of the superior colliculus are expected to cause an incongruous contralateral homonymous hemianopic field defect AND a contralateral afferent pupillary defect. The afferent input to the pupillary light reflex, however, separates from the visual pathways just anterior to the lateral geniculate nucleus. Therefore, retrogeniculate optic pathway lesions AND pure lateral geniculate nucleus lesions (not involving the optic tract) do not affect pupillary function. Lesions in this area would affect the fibers that carry visual information from the superior right quadrant of the visual field in both eyes. As a result, a homonymous right superior quadrantanopia would be expected, not an inferior quadrantanopia. Option C - A monocular right inferior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Monocular field defects are not caused by lesions in the brain but rather by abnormalities in the eye itself or along the optic nerve. The lesion described in the question is located in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe, which is a cerebral region. Therefore, monocular field defects would not be expected. Option D - A monocular right superior quadrantanopia in the right eye only: Similar to option C, monocular field defects are not caused by cerebral lesions. A lesion in the anterior portion of the left temporal lobe would not result in a monocular field defect in the right eye. Option E - A left afferent pupillary defect: Afferent pupillary defects (also known as a Marcus Gunn pupil) are typically caused by lesions affecting the optic nerve or severe retinal disease in the eye. The lesion described in the question is not located along the optic nerve, and it would not cause an afferent pupillary defect. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old man presented in the ER with a complaint of muscle weakness, and increased heart rate for the past 7 days. Investigation revealed serum bicarbonate:14 mmol/L, Anion Gap is normal. Urine analysis shows no cast, pus cells, or crystals but the pH of urine is 5.2. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type II is suspected. Which part of the nephron is most likely to be involved in the above-mentioned condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man presented in the ER with a complaint of muscle weakness, and increased heart rate for the past 7 days. Investigation revealed serum bicarbonate:14 mmol/L, Anion Gap is normal. Urine analysis shows no cast, pus cells, or crystals but the pH of urine is 5.2. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis type II is suspected. Which part of the nephron is most likely to be involved in the above-mentioned condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Proximal convoluted tubule A renal tubular acidosis is a group of diseases that results in the inability of the kidneys to excrete acids out of the blood into the urine. As a result of it, metabolic acidosis results. In Renal tubular acidosis type 2, the proximal convoluted tubule is involved which results in the inability to reabsorb the bicarbonate ions leading to metabolic acidosis. However, the distal tubules are working normally and can acidify the urine. That is why metabolic acidosis is less severe. Hypokalemia is also associated with renal tubular acidosis. Some of the symptoms of renal tubular acidosis type 2 are palpitations, irregular heartbeats, paralysis, and death. In RTA type 2, there are low levels of potassium and bicarbonate. Incorrect options: Option A: Early distal tubule The early distal tubule is affected in renal tubular acidosis type 1, in which there is an inability to excrete acid from the body. It can be inherited from parents or it can be associated with autoimmune conditions like systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus, etc. Renal tubular acidosis type 1 patients are prone to kidney stones. Option B: Capillaries In renal tubular acidosis, capillaries are not the cause of metabolic acidosis. Capillaries surround the nephrons and are involved in providing the blood supply and also reabsorb the molecules so that they can be recirculated in the blood. The obstruction of the capillaries can lead to acute kidney injury. Option D: Collecting duct The collecting duct is the last part of the nephron which reabsorbs the water and electrolytes to concentrate the urine. It also excretes waste materials. The collecting duct is mainly controlled by ADH and aldosterone. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes presents with nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Labs reveal blood glucose of 460 mg/dL, pH of 7.20, and potassium of 2.2 mEq/L. Urinalysis is positive for ketones. What is the most appropriate initial intervention?
questions.solution: Correct Option A. Administer 0.45% NaCl infusion: This is the correct initial intervention. The patient is presenting with diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), which is characterized by hyperglycemia, ketosis, and metabolic acidosis. The low blood pH (7.20) indicates acidosis. The patient's low potassium level (2.2 mEq/L) suggests hypokalemia, likely due to intracellular shifts of potassium as a result of acidosis. Administering a 0.45% NaCl (normal saline) infusion helps to correct dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and acidosis. It also assists in improving tissue perfusion. After initiating fluid resuscitation, insulin administration can be started to help lower blood glucose levels and further correct acidosis Incorrect options: Option B. Administer potassium chloride: While hypokalemia (low potassium) is a potential complication of diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), administering potassium chloride as the initial intervention can be dangerous. The patient's potassium level is already low (2.2 mEq/L), and administering potassium without proper fluid resuscitation can lead to further imbalances and potentially life-threatening cardiac arrhythmias. Correcting fluid balance is the priority before addressing potassium imbalances. Option C. Administer 0.1 units/kg IV insulin: While insulin administration is a crucial component of DKA treatment, it should not be the initial step in this case. Before insulin is administered, it's important to address the patient's fluid and electrolyte imbalances. Administering insulin without adequate hydration can lead to further decreases in potassium levels and potential complications. Option D. Administer a dextrose solution: Administering a dextrose solution is not appropriate as the initial intervention for DKA. The patient's blood glucose level is already very high (460 mg/dL), and giving more glucose can exacerbate the hyperglycemia and worsen the acidosis. The primary concern in DKA management is first addressing fluid and electrolyte imbalances. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.stemHtml: A second-year medical student learns about the regulation and function of prolactin in his endocrinology lecture. Which of the following dopaminergic pathway is involved in the secretion of prolactin?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Tuberoinfundibular: Prolactin is secreted by the anterior pituitary gland . Its secretion is inhibited by the production of dopamine by the tuberoinfundibular pathway of the hypothalamus . Decreased activity of this pathway results in increased production of prolactin. Thyroid-releasing hormone (TRH) can also stimulate the production of prolactin in conditions like primary or secondary hypothyroidism. Prolactin can inhibit its own secretion by increasing dopamine production from the hypothalamus. Functions of prolactin include: Stimulation of milk production Inhibition of ovulation (females) Inhibition of spermatogenesis (males) Dopamine agonists (cabergoline) are used to treat conditions in which prolactin excess (prolactinoma). Drugs like antipsychotics and antidepressants can decrease dopamine production and can result in an increase in prolactin levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Mesocortical: Decreased activity of the mesocortical pathway results in negative symptoms like anergia and apathy. It is affected minimally by antipsychotics. Option B - Mesolimbic: Increased activity of the mesolimbic pathway results in positive symptoms like delusions and hallucinations. Antipsychotics have a marked effect on these pathways. Option C - Nigrostriatal: Decreased activity of nigrostriatal pathways results in extrapyramidal symptoms like dystonia and parkinsonism. It is notably affected by movement disorders. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Dilation of bronchi with thickened walls
questions.solution: Correct Option A - Dilation of bronchi with thickened walls: The defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis is the dilation of bronchi with thickened walls. Bronchiectasis is a chronic respiratory disease characterized by the irreversible dilation and thickening of the bronchial walls due to recurrent infections, inflammation, or obstruction. This leads to the accumulation of mucus and impaired clearance, leading to recurrent lung infections and chronic cough. The dilation of bronchi can be seen in imaging studies like chest X-rays, CT scans, or bronchograms Incorrect Options: Option B - Increased numbers of alveoli in the lungs: Increased numbers of alveoli in the lungs is not a morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis because Bronchiectasis is a condition that primarily affects the bronchi, which are the large airways that lead from the trachea to the lungs Alveoli are small air sacs within the lungs where gas exchange occurs. They are not directly affected by Bronchiectasis, although if the condition is severe and chronic, it can eventually damage the alveoli and other lung structures. The primary morphological characteristics of Bronchiectasis are related to the bronchial walls, including dilation, thickening, and scarring. Option C - Presence of fluid-filled cavities in the lungs: Presence of fluid-filled cavities in the lungs is not a defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis. Cysts or cavities are sometimes observed in patients with Bronchiectasis, but this is not always true. Option D - Presence of nodules in the lungs: Presence of nodules in the lungs is not a defining morphological characteristic of Bronchiectasis. Nodules may be seen in patients with other lung conditions, such as tuberculosis or lung cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

It has a relatively shorter half-life compared to other IgG subclasses and is associated with acute infections. questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old male patient came to the emergency department with complaints of palpitations and sickness for the past 2 weeks. The patient has no significant history. The ECG showed bradycardia and long pauses between heartbeats. Which of the following is the diagnosis of this patient’s condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option A- Sick sinus syndrome: Sick sinus syndrome is a disorder of the sinus, which normally controls the rate and rhythm of the heart. Sick sinus syndrome presents with the symptoms of palpitations, dizziness, and fatigue. It also causes bradycardia and tachycardia. Pauses can occur in which there is no atrial or ventricular activity. Most common cause of sick sinus node syndrome is age-related wear and tear of heart tissues. With age, there is generation of the tissue, and the conduction can also be affected. On ECG, one can find bradycardia, irregular beats, or long pauses between the heartbeats. Some of the risk factors for heart disease include high blood pressure, lack of exercise, high cholesterol, etc. The ECG and Holter monitoring can diagnose this condition. This condition is treated with regular checkups. Medications are also used to treat this condition. Pacemaker and catheter ablation may be needed. Incorrect Options: Option B- Medication-induced hypotension: Certain medications can also cause palpitations and syncope due to vasodilation or decreased cardiac output. Some of the medications are diuretics, vasodilators (both arteriodilators and venodilators), beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, etc. In old age people, an antihistamine can also cause dizziness and syncope. This can predispose patients to fall-related fractures. However, this patient's history is not significant for taking any medications. Option C- Carotid stenosis: Carotid stenosis is also common in the elderly population and can cause transient ischaemic attack and syncope due to the obstruction of the blood supply to the brain. However, this patient's ECG is consistent with the diagnosis of sick sinus syndrome, in which there can be bradycardia, long pauses between heartbeats, and irregular beats. Option D- Aortic stenosis: Aortic stenosis is common after 60 years of age. Similarly, patients with bicuspid aortic valves are predisposed to aortic stenosis. Aortic stenosis can result in decreased blood being pumped into the aorta and can result in syncope. Diuretics, vasodilators, and other drugs can also add to the effect and can result in syncope and drowsiness. This patient is not suffering from aortic stenosis. Aortic valve diameter can be seen on echocardiography. @Neet_pg_bot

Option D - Methylprednisolone: Methylprednisolone is a glucocorticoid (similar to cortisol) and is not used as a first-line treatment for ACTH-secreting pituitary adenomas. questions.stem: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following does not correspond to brainstem death?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Absence of toe jerk: Brain death is when functional brainstem death occurs permanently such that consciousness and spontaneous respiration are impossible . Certain preconditions have to be met for the diagnosis of brain death: The patient must have undergone severe brain damage of known cause Is highly unconscious and unresponsive Requires ventilation No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation. Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies With the satisfaction of preconditions, a formal assessment of the brainstem reflexes can be performed. These are to be performed by two clinicians not associated with the transplant team on two separate occasions. The absence of cranial reflexes, motor responses, and spontaneous respiration characterises brain death. An absence of a motor response to painful stimuli to the head/face or within the cranial nerve distribution to adequate stimulation of any somatic area indicates brainstem death. Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex: The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death. These reflexes are: Pupillary Corneal Gag (pharyngeal) Tracheal (cough) Oculovestibular (caloric) Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration: The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner: Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration. During this time, the arterial PO 2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg ) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation. 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea. Option D - Absence of cough: A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death. @Neet_pg_bot

    • Is highly unconscious and unresponsive
    • Requires ventilation
    • No known CNS depressants and muscle relaxants are causing the clinical presentation.
    • Absence of low body temperature, severe hypotension and metabolic or hormonal pathologies

  • Spinal reflexes such as toe or finger movements do not indicate brainstem death.

 

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Absence of pupillary reflex:

  • The absence of cranial nerve reflexes characterises brainstem death.
  • These reflexes are:
    • Pupillary
    • Corneal
    • Gag (pharyngeal)
    • Tracheal (cough)
    • Oculovestibular (caloric)

Option B - Absence of spontaneous respiration:

  • The absence of spontaneous respiration characterises brainstem death which is checked in the following manner:
    • Pre Ventilation with 100% oxygen is given for a minimum of 5 minutes. Then, the patient is detached from the ventilator for 10 minutes to confirm the absence of respiration.
    • During this time, the arterial PO2 must be >8kPa (60 mmHg) to ensure adequate respiratory stimulation.
    • 6L/min oxygen is delivered through the endotracheal catheter to prevent hypoxia during the apnoea.

  • A cough or tracheal reflex is a cranial reflex which characterises brainstem death.

questions.stem: Which of the following study biases would best be described by an incorrect calculation of mortality rate as a result of deaths which are estimated by a prevalence of a slowly progressive disease using a time interval which is short?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following study biases would best be described by an incorrect calculation of mortality rate as a result of deaths which are estimated by a prevalence of a slowly progressive disease using a time interval which is short?
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Length-time bias: Length-time bias is an error which occurs due to measuring a time interval which is to short, possible over-representing longer disease processes. This error is especially applicable to lung cancers, which have a wide variability of growth rates. Incorrect Options: Option A - Centripetal bias: Centripetal bias occurs when a study cohort is analyzed through a specific institution or center that may not be representative of the broader population. This can lead to biased results that may not be applicable to the general population. Option B - Lead-time bias: Lead-time bias occurs when a disease is detected earlier through screening or diagnostic tests, but this early detection does not necessarily lead to improved outcomes. This bias can make it appear that a screening test is effective in prolonging survival, when in fact, it may only be detecting the disease earlier without providing any actual benefit in terms of survival. Option D - Reporting bias: Reporting bias refers to the selective inclusion or exclusion of results in a study, which can lead to a distortion of the true relationship between variables. This bias can arise if researchers or journals choose to publish only positive or significant results, while neglecting to publish negative or non-significant findings. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best reflects our current understanding of the physiology of the pleural space?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements best reflects our current understanding of the physiology of the pleural space?

options.label: A
options.text: Absorption of pleural fluid is effectuated by uptake by capillaries

options.label: B
options.text: Liquid, proteins, and other molecules are actively transported through mesothelial cells into the pleural space

options.label: C
options.text: Pressure gradient between the pleural space and interstitial space in which the intrapleural pressure > interstitial pressure

options.label: D
options.text: Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively

questions.answerText: Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Molecules, proteins, and liquid move passively: The pleural space consists of two cellular layers, a superficially located mesothelial layer and an underlying connective tissue layer. These membrane have been shown to be leaky, enabling the occurrence of passive movement of molecules, proteins, and liquid. Incorrect Options: Option A - Absorption of pleural fluid by capillary uptake: Pleural fluid absorption is mainly carried out through lymphatic vessels in the parietal pleura, not capillaries. The movement of fluid into the capillaries is driven by oncotic pressure rather than by an active process. Option B - Active transport of liquid, proteins, and other molecules through mesothelial cells: The mesothelial cells in the pleura do not actively transport liquid, proteins, and other molecules into the pleural space. Fluid accumulation in the pleural space is primarily due to alterations in hydrostatic and oncotic pressures, and the permeability of the pleura, allowing for passive flow. Option C - Pressure gradient between the pleural space and interstitial space where the intrapleural pressure is greater than the interstitial pressure: This is not accurate. The pressure within the pleural space (intrapleural pressure) is generally negative (or less than atmospheric pressure) to maintain lung expansion. It's not greater than the interstitial pressure. The negative pressure facilitates the passive flow of fluid from the interstitial space into the pleural space. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old male industrial worker comes to the clinic complaining of wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath for the last six months. Recently, he went to Dubai for a holiday and did not experience any symptoms and was completely fine. Spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with a 15% increase in FEV1 after bronchodilator administration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old male industrial worker comes to the clinic complaining of wheezing, coughing, and shortness of breath for the last six months. Recently, he went to Dubai for a holiday and did not experience any symptoms and was completely fine. Spirometry shows an obstructive pattern with a 15% increase in FEV1 after bronchodilator administration. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Occupational asthma: Occupational asthma is caused by exposure to substances at the workplace. These substances can trigger an immune response in the respiratory system, leading to inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Common agents associated with occupational asthma include flour and grain dust, wood dust, aldehydes, latex, and isocyanates. Clinical features of occupational asthma include the following: Cough, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. These symptoms usually occur during work and may improve when the person is away from work or on vacation. Over time, if exposure to the agent continues, the symptoms may worsen and become persistent, even when the person is away from work. Diagnosis: A detailed medical history can help in making the diagnosis of occupational asthma. Pulmonary function tests show decreased FEV1 and FEV1/FVC ratio. There is an increase of > 12% in FEV1 on bronchodilator administration. Incorrect Options: Option A - Allergic rhinitis: Allergic rhinitis is an allergic reaction that affects the nasal passages. It occurs in response to allergens (e.g., pollen, dust mites, or animal dander). Symptoms include nasal congestion, runny nose, sneezing, and itching. The clinical symptoms of this patient are not consistent with allergic rhinitis. Option B - Emphysema: Emphysema is a type of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) that causes damage to the air sacs in the lungs. It is typically caused by long-term exposure to cigarette smoke. Symptoms include shortness of breath, wheezing, and chronic cough. In emphysema, there is a < 12% increase in FEV1 on bronchodilator administration. Option C - Chronic bronchitis: Chronic bronchitis is a chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) involving inflammation and narrowing of the airways. Chronic bronchitis is characterised by a productive cough for at least three months in each of two consecutive years. This condition is typically caused by exposure to irritants such as cigarette smoke, air pollution, occupational dust, and chemicals. There is a < 12% increase in FEV1 on bronchodilator administration in chronic bronchitis. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: A

options.label: B
options.text: Airway narrowing due to inflammation and oedema of the airway epithelium

options.label: C
options.text: Increased airway resistance due to a decrease in surfactant production

questions.answerText: Airway narrowing due to inflammation and oedema of the airway epithelium
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Airway narrowing due to inflammation and oedema of the airway epithelium: Exercise-induced asthma (EIA), also known as exercise-induced bronchoconstriction (EIB), is a type of asthma triggered by physical activity. During exercise, increased ventilation and airway cooling can cause the airways to narrow, leading to symptoms such as coughing, wheezing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. The exact mechanism behind EIA is not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to the release of inflammatory mediators such as histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins from mast cells and other cells in the airways. These mediators cause bronchoconstriction and inflammation in the airways, leading to the symptoms of EIA. Management of EIA involves avoiding triggers and using medications to prevent symptoms. Pre-exercise use of a short-acting beta-agonist (SABA) inhaler, such as albuterol, can help prevent symptoms in many cases. In addition, warming up before exercise, exercising in warm and humid environments, and wearing a face mask or scarf over the mouth and nose can also help reduce symptoms. Option C - Increased airway resistance due to a decrease in surfactant production: Surfactant is a substance that reduces surface tension within the alveoli and helps prevent them from collapsing. It is not directly related to the pathophysiology of exercise-induced asthma. Option D - Airway obstruction due to mucus hypersecretion: Mucus hypersecretion is a feature of chronic bronchitis, but it is not a prominent feature of exercise-induced asthma. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D - Gaucher disease: Gaucher disease is a rare genetic disorder caused by the deficiency of an enzyme called glucocerebrosidase, leading to the accumulation of a substance called glucocerebroside in cells, particularly macrophages. This buildup can cause enlargement of the spleen (splenomegaly) and may result in symptoms like fatigue, weakness, and a feeling of fullness in the abdomen due to the enlarged spleen. Laboratory findings can include anemia and thrombocytopenia due to the sequestration of blood cells in the spleen. Incorrect Options: Option A - Rheumatoid arthritis: Rheumatoid arthritis is an autoimmune disorder primarily affecting the joints. It typically does not cause symptoms like fatigue, weakness, or splenomegaly (enlarged spleen). Laboratory findings in rheumatoid arthritis are more focused on autoimmune markers and inflammatory markers rather than anemia and thrombocytopenia. Option B - Infectious mononucleosis (EBV): Infectious mononucleosis, caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), can lead to symptoms such as fatigue, weakness, and splenomegaly. However, the key differentiating feature in this case is the presence of normocytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. These findings are not characteristic of EBV infection. Option C - Thalassemia major: Thalassemia major is a genetic disorder characterized by abnormal hemoglobin production, leading to chronic anemia. While it can cause fatigue and weakness due to the anemia, it typically does not result in a palpable spleen well below the left costal margin. Thalassemia major is not associated with thrombocytopenia or a feeling of fullness in the abdomen. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of severe eczema, recurrent pyogenic infections, and bleeding episodes. Physical examination reveals eczematous skin lesions, petechiae, and small platelets on peripheral smear. Laboratory tests show low IgG and IgM levels, along with increased IgE and IgA. Which of the following immunodeficiency syndromes is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 4-month-old male infant is brought to the pediatrician with complaints of severe eczema, recurrent pyogenic infections, and bleeding episodes. Physical examination reveals eczematous skin lesions, petechiae, and small platelets on peripheral smear. Laboratory tests show low IgG and IgM levels, along with increased IgE and IgA. Which of the following immunodeficiency syndromes is most likely responsible for this presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option D - Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome is an X-linked immunodeficiency disorder characterized by the triad of eczema, recurrent infections, and thrombocytopenia (low platelet count). Patients with Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome often have bleeding episodes due to the combination of low platelet counts and platelet dysfunction. They also have increased IgE levels, which can contribute to the development of eczema. The syndrome is caused by mutations in the gene encoding the Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome protein (WASP), which plays a crucial role in cytoskeletal organization and immune cell function. Incorrect Options: Option A - X-Linked Bruton's Disease (X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia): X-Linked Bruton’s Disease, also known as X-Linked Agammaglobulinemia (XLA), is characterized by a deficiency in B cells and a lack of antibodies (IgG, IgA, and IgM). However, the presentation described in the question includes increased levels of IgE and IgA, which is not consistent with XLA. In XLA, patients would be prone to recurrent bacterial infections but would not have bleeding episodes or increased IgE levels. questions.stem: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is a condition in which there is the inappropriate secretion of ADH which results in impaired excretion of water from the kidneys. This condition leads to which of the following abnormalities ?
questions.stemHtml: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is a condition in which there is the inappropriate secretion of ADH which results in impaired excretion of water from the kidneys. This condition leads to which of the following abnormalities ?
questions.solution: Correct Option B - Hyponatremia: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is a condition in which there is the inappropriate secretion of ADH which results in impaired excretion of water from the kidneys. This condition usually leads to hyponatremia . There are many different types of hyponatremia. The hyponatremia which is caused by to syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is normovolemic hyponatremia . Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion can be caused due to central nervous system causes, neoplastic diseases, and chest infections. The central nervous system causes include meningitis, stroke, and tumors. The neoplastic causes include small-cell lung cancer and chest infection including pneumonia and tuberculosis. This disease is diagnosed on the basis of elevated urine osmolality and urine sodium levels. The most accurate test for this disease is ADH level . It is usually elevated in SIADH. It is managed by treating the underlying cause. The underlying cause may include nephrogenic diabetes insipidus for which demeclocycline is used. If there is resistant hyponatremia and tolvaptan is used. The fluid is usually restricted between 500 to 1000 ml per day . Incorrect Options: Option A - Hypokalemia: Hypokalemia can result when there is excessive renal loss which can be due to many conditions including Cushing syndrome, hyperaldosteronism and renal tubular acidosis . It is not caused by the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion. Option C - Hyperammonemia: Ammonia is a byproduct of nitrogenous waste . Hyperammonemia occurs when there is liver failure. In chronic liver diseases, the liver is unable to convert ammonia into urea . Thus, it accumulates in the blood causing hepatic encephalopathy. Option D - Hyperglycemia: Hyperglycemia is the accumulation of excess glucose in the blood . It is usually seen in diabetes mellitus. Its clinical features include polyuria, polydipsia and polyphagia . Prolonged hyperglycemia can lead to peripheral neuropathy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Obtain radiograph and hand surgery consult in ED
questions.solution: Correct Option C - Obtain radiograph and hand surgery consult in ED: High-pressure injections with paint, oil, hydraulic fluid, or other fluids are high-risk surgical emergencies . These injuries often appear unimpressive initially but will progress to edema, ischemic injury, and compartment syndrome due to inflammation. A radiograph can sometimes show radiopaque substances such as lead-based paint. The injury should be immobilized and elevated, and the patient should receive a tetanus shot and antibiotics. Hand surgery needs to be immediately consulted, as treatment involves early surgical debridement and decompression. Incorrect Options: Option A - Order radiograph to look for foreign body: This patient should have a radiograph, but hand surgery also needs to be consulted. Option B - Give tetanus shot and discharge for follow-up with hand surgery tomorrow: Tetanus vaccination should be provided, but this patient should not be discharged and needs to see a hand surgeon in the ED promptly. Option D - Administer local wound care and pain control: Wound care and pain control are insufficient treatments for this injury. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 6 year-old-boy, with a known case of sickle cell anemia, is brought to the Hospital by his parents with the complaint of irritability, muscle weakness and pain, lethargy and palpitations. On examination, there was pallor, heart rate:102 beats /min, respiratory rate: 28/min, B.P:90/65mmHg. Laboratory findings include serum sodium:142 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2mmol/L, serum chloride:107 mmol/L, serum Bicarbonate:15 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas shows pH:7.21. Urine analysis findings include pH 5.9, no casts, RBCs, WBCs, or protein. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis is suspected. Which of the following is associated with this patient's condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 6 year-old-boy, with a known case of sickle cell anemia, is brought to the Hospital by his parents with the complaint of irritability, muscle weakness and pain, lethargy and palpitations. On examination, there was pallor, heart rate:102 beats /min, respiratory rate: 28/min, B.P:90/65mmHg. Laboratory findings include serum sodium:142 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2mmol/L, serum chloride:107 mmol/L, serum Bicarbonate:15 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas shows pH:7.21. Urine analysis findings include pH 5.9, no casts, RBCs, WBCs, or protein. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis is suspected. Which of the following is associated with this patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Normal anion gap Renal tubular acidosis is due to the inability of the kidney to either excrete hydrogen ions or reabsorb filtered bicarbonate. There are many types of RTA including type 1 RTA, type 2 RTA, and type 4 RTA. Type 1 RTA is due to the inability of the distal tubule of the nephron to excrete hydrogen ions leading to metabolic acidosis. Causes of RTA include primary causes: familial, and idiopathic. Secondary causes include sickle cell anemia, autoimmune (SLE, Sjogren's), hyperparathyroidism, and Vitamin D intoxication, chronic hepatitis, renal transplantation. Anion Gap is used to find the cause of metabolic acidosis. The normal value of the anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L. Normal anion gap with metabolic acidosis is due to loss of bicarbonate by the kidney( RTA type 1 and RTA type 2) or gut (Diarrhea). Symptoms include increased respiratory rate, irregular heart rate, muscle weakness, lethargy, constipation, nephrocalcinosis, paralysis, and death. There will be hyperkalemia due to hyperaldosteronism. Incorrect options: Option A: High anion gap metabolic acidosis Conditions with Metabolic acidosis associated with high anion gap include methanol, uremia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paracetamol, paraldehyde, isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates etc. (MUDPILES). Option C: Decreased anion gap metabolic acidosis Though not related to acid-base balance, it could signal disease. Conditions with abnormally low anion gap include low serum albumin, increased chloride, hyperkalemia, hypercalcemia, and multiple myeloma. Option D: Metabolic alkalosis Metabolic alkalosis results when there is an increase in bicarbonate ions or a decrease in hydrogen ions. In renal tubular acidosis, there is metabolic acidosis. Some of the causes of metabolic alkalosis are vomiting, diuretics, and hyperaldosteronism. @Neet_pg_bot
